The paper was submitted to the Journal of Computational Physics on July 7, 2023
The research involves collaboration between Aix Marseille University, CNRS, Centrale Marseille, Imperial College London, and Institut Fresnel
The wavelength used in simulations is 500 nm
The mesh refinement uses triangular elements with side length λ/6 in free-space and λ/12 in the cloak and protected zone
Three discrete permittivity values {7, 10, 12} are used in the ternary search space
The protection criterion C₁ is defined as the integral of |u|² over the protected region S₁
The invisibility criterion C₂ measures the integral of |u - u₀|² over the free-space region S₂
The chaotic ternary grey wolf optimizer (CTGWO) uses a modulo operator to enforce contributions to remain in [0:2]
The standard GWO parameter 'a' decreases linearly from 2 to 0 across iterations according to a = 2(1 - iter/T_max)
The paper considers both discrete ternary search spaces and continuous search spaces where permittivity can take any real value in [7:12]
NSGA-II hierarchizes domination levels with multiple Pareto fronts
Crowding distances in NSGA-II are calculated criterion-by-criterion to maintain solution diversity
The scalar Helmholtz equation formulation applies equivalently to acoustic, elastic, and electromagnetic wave problems
The paper divides the wolf pack into two groups: one for exploration and one for exploitation
The contribution of a leader in CTGWO is computed using the formula: yᵢₗ(iter) = (xᵢₗ - bᵢdᵢₗ(iter)) mod 2
The paper aims to estimate a very elevated number of parameters compared to previous works like reference [17]
The position update in standard GWO is computed as the average of three leader contributions: xq(iter+1) = (1/3)(yα + yβ + yδ)
The vectors b and c in GWO are calculated as b = 2a ⊙ r₁ - a and c = 2r₂, where r₁ and r₂ have random components between 0 and 1
The Hadamard (component-wise) product is denoted by ⊙ in the paper's notation
Second-order Lagrange elements are used in the finite element discretization
The implementation follows methods described in reference [20] and uses ONELAB open-source tutorials
GmshRead[] and ScalarField[] functions are used to control discrete values throughout optimization
The paper addresses the fundamental trade-off where infinite conducting boundaries ensure protection but cause large scattering
Impedance matching between regions provides invisibility but eliminates protection
The paper proposes using nature-inspired optimizers (GWO and genetic algorithms) rather than deductive reasoning for cloak design
The computational domain is surrounded by PMLs (Perfectly Matched Layers) that model an unbounded medium
